new_statements.quote: 1. Phonetics 1a. Vowels Santandrea records five vowel phonemes for NDOGO-SERE, i € a9 u, with sub- sidiary values I e O U in unstressed syllables. Hackett, however, records at least seven vowel phonemes for Congo SERE. [...] 2. Tone and Stress 2a. There appear to be three main tone levels in these languages—High, Mid, and Low. Rising and Falling tones are common outside NDOGO-SERE, but seem for the most part to be the result of assimilation. [...] 2b. Stress is often responsible for changes in vowel quality and vowel length. In MAYOGO there is a tendency towards vowel length on the penultimate syllable. In NGBAKA, GBAYA, and BANDA, on the other hand, there is a tendency towards extra shortness here.

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (no catalog record, no statement held by the project). Adds type only: 3-level tone language with stressed vs unstressed syllables (vowel reduction when unstressed); NO placement of word stress for Sere. Consistent with the earlier sere1264 reader and the ndog1248/bela1255/mund1326 sibling checks, all snippet-only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ndogo-Sere (Sudan Sere, after Santandrea) has three level tones (High, Mid, Low; contour tones mainly outside Ndogo-Sere, by assimilation); the five vowels take lax subsidiary values in UNSTRESSED syllables, so word stress is presupposed, but the chapter nowhere says on which syllable Sere/Ndogo-Sere stress falls: sec. 2b gives placement-related tendencies only for Mayogo (penultimate length) and Ngbaka/Gbaya/Banda (penultimate extra-shortness). Hackett's 'Congo SERE' is mentioned only for its seven-vowel inventory.
new_statements.exceptions: none for Sere; whole-volume full-text probes for NDOGO-SERE/SERE with stress/stressed/accent/penultimate/first syllable return only other chapters' 2b paragraphs (Moru, Ma'di, Mangbetu, Bilin) and the p. 86 vowel remark
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 write 'NDOGO-SERE' for the Sudan cluster described by Santandrea (Ndogo, Sere, Bai, Bviri around Wau) and separately cite Hackett's 'Congo SERE' (seven vowels); Tucker 1940 treats 'the Ndogo-Sere group (Belanda-Basiri)' at group level from his own Wau phonetic/vocabulary notes plus Santandrea's manuscript. Statements are group-level (Ndogo-Sere), not specific to a Sere dialect.
